item.title: First HH-60W Arrives at Andrews for Contingency Response, VIP Transport
item.dc:creator: Greg Hadley
item.description:
Like a new car from the dealership, an HH-60W helicopter touched down at Joint Base Andrews, Md., on Nov. 2 with paperwork, a set of keys, and that fresh-from-the-factory smell. The newly activated 5th Helicopter Squadron accepted its first “Whiskey” in a brief but pomp-filled ceremony attended by the Air Force Undersecretary Matthew Lohmeier and Vice Chief of Staff Gen. John D. Lamontagne. The 5th and its sister unit, the 1st Helicopter Squadron, will eventually have 26 HH-60Ws to replace the current fleet of UH-1N Hueys that have flown executive airlift and contingency response missions over the nation’s capital since 1971.

The post First HH-60W Arrives at Andrews for Contingency Response, VIP Transport appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine.
item.content:encoded:
JOINT BASE ANDREWS, Md.—Like a new car from the dealership, the HH-60W helicopter that touched down here Nov. 2 came with paperwork, a set of keys, and that fresh-from-the-factory smell.

It’s the first time helicopter pilots at Andrews have smelled that smell in 55 years.

The newly activated 5th Helicopter Squadron accepted its first “Whiskey” in a brief but pomp-filled ceremony attended by the Undersecretary of Air Force Matthew Lohmeier and Vice Chief of Staff Gen. John D. Lamontagne. The 5th and its sister unit, the 1st Helicopter Squadron, will eventually have 26 HH-60Ws to replace the current fleet of UH-1N Hueys that have flown executive airlift and contingency response missions over the nation’s capital since 1971.

The Huey achieved iconic status during the Vietnam War, but Air Force officials say it’s long past time to replace the ones at Andrews with a more capable aircraft. The HH-60W’s primary mission is combat search and rescue, and it can fly 25 percent faster and 100 percent farther than the UH-1N while lifting 200 percent more. It also has a bigger cabin, modern avionics, and a glass cockpit.

The HH-60Ws at Andrews will eventually be slightly modified for the D.C. mission. But the first one to touch down Nov. 2 came directly from manufacturer Sikorsky’s factory in Connecticut, untouched. Chief Master Sgt. Benjamin Griffin, the 316th Operations Group’s command chief, handed off the DD250 acceptance form to Lt. Col. Zachary Tindall, the 316th’s maintenance operations flight commander. Col. Kevin Geoffroy, commander of the 316th, handed off the keys to Lt. Col. Jonathan Bonilla, commander of the 5th Helicopter Squadron.

The keys came with a clickable seagull keychain—a nod to the seagull on the 5th Helicopter Squadron’s emblem, drawn from its lineage as the 5th Emergency Rescue Squadron.

After the ceremony, Airmen and visitors swarmed the new Whiskey, checking out its refueling probe and its gun mounts (to be removed). Lamontagne clambered into the cockpit at one point.

It’s been a long and winding journey to get a new helicopter to Andrews. In the late 2000s and early 2010s, the Common Vertical Lift Support Platform program was supposed to produce a helicopter to replace the UH-1N. After that program was canceled, the Air Force pivoted around 2018 to developing the MH-139 Grey Wolf, a modified commercial helicopter, for both ICBM security forces and the executive airlift/contingency response mission. Budgetary and programmatic developments led the service to abandon those plans last July and pivot once more to the HH-60W.

“Talk to a bunch of different individuals in the community, and you’ll realize that this has been something that has been thought about for quite a bit of time,” Bonilla said. “And the fact that it’s here is just making a lot of people smile.”

Col. Karl W. Seekamp, commander of the 316th Wing, spoke during the ceremony of just how necessary for the UH-1N to make way for the HH-60W.

“For a moment, I’d ask you to visualize the Andrews flight line 55 years ago, when this unit was operating HH-3 Jolly Greens and our current fleet of UH-1Ns,” Seekamp told the audience. “At that time, you would have seen massive piston-driven C-124s on the ramp. On the Navy ramp would have been Skyraiders and Neptunes. The 113th Wing would have recently upgraded from its Super Sabers to F-105 Thunderchiefs. And of course, on the west ramp of the 89th Airlift Wing, you would see President Nixon’s special airlift mission Boeing 707, the first Air Force One to wear the blue and white paint scheme. These aircraft were once the best in the world, unrivaled technology—but that was a long time ago.”

It’ll be a while still before the Huey is completely gone. Because the contingency response mission is 24/7, the 316th Wing can’t just retire its UH-1Ns and then make the preparations to transition to the HH-60W, like most units do when they’re getting a new aircraft. Instead, the 1st Helicopter Squadron will continue to handle the day-to-day mission with the UH-1N while the 5th Helicopter Squadron gets up to speed on the HH-60W.

Already, the 5th has spent two months prepping for the Whiskey, Bonilla said, describing “a lot of tasks that may seem trivial initially, but all of those tasks are extremely important so that we can actually fly the helicopter: … making sure that all the systems are here, making sure that all the equipment is here, looking at the hangar space, looking at the mission planning, ensuring that all the aircrew is ready to go, has been vetted, has been checked, and they have the proper experience.”

In January, the first group of UH-1N aviators will start training to transition to the HH-60W. Maintainers will also start training on the aircraft. For now, the need to start that training is greater than the need to make modifications, Bonilla said.

One thing that won’t be modified, he noted, is the paint job. While the Huey sports a distinctive dark blue, gold, and white livery, the Whiskey will remain gunship grey so that it remains available for the combat rescue mission.

The post First HH-60W Arrives at Andrews for Contingency Response, VIP Transport appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine.

item.title: US Conducts Airstrikes on Iran, Latest in Series of Undisclosed Attacks
item.dc:creator: Chris Gordon
item.description:
The U.S. conducted limited airstrikes against Iran on Nov. 2, the latest in a series of attacks the U.S. military has undertaken in the past few weeks but not publicly disclosed. The strikes occurred just ahead of the U.S. midterm elections.

The post US Conducts Airstrikes on Iran, Latest in Series of Undisclosed Attacks appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine.
item.content:encoded:
The U.S. conducted limited airstrikes against Iran on Nov. 2, the latest in a series of attacks the U.S. military has undertaken in the past few weeks but not publicly disclosed. The strikes occurred just ahead of the U.S. midterm elections.

President Donald Trump acknowledged the latest strikes in an interview on Nov. 3.

“It was just a minor attack; it wasn’t war,” Trump said on Fox News. “They built an anti-aircraft facility. It took them about two months. We watched it get built. As soon as it was completed, we hit it last night very nicely.” 

Iranian forces fired at U.S. aircraft on Nov. 2, U.S. officials said, and Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps claimed to have shot down a U.S. Air Force MQ-9 Reaper. But no U.S. aircraft are believed to have been downed, a U.S. official said.

The latest attacks took place on Qeshm Island, which hosts Iranian military sites and has been a frequent target of U.S. attacks. It sits in the Persian Gulf just outside the critical chokepoint of the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran has repeatedly attacked commercial shipping since the U.S.-Iran war began in February, seeking to impose economic and diplomatic costs on the U.S. and its partners.

The last publicly announced strikes occurred in early September, when the U.S. attacked five Iranian tankers in response to attempted Iranian strikes on U.S. military vessels. Iran retaliated with a missile attack on Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan, a key base for the U.S., where it damaged some U.S. aircraft.

But the U.S. military has been conducting some airstrikes since then, U.S. officials told Air & Space Forces Magazine. The strikes have been limited in nature and have included targets such as air defenses and other facilities.

A spokesperson for U.S. Central Command declined to comment. The airstrikes were first reported by The Wall Street Journal.

The U.S. military engaged in smaller-scale strikes during tit-for-tat exchanges during a ceasefire that ended the all-out U.S. and Israeli strike campaign, Operation Epic Fury, in April. Since then, the U.S. has maintained firepower in the region as part of a military pressure campaign and blockade of Iranian ports.

The Trump administration has also tightened sanctions against Iran and attempted to help commercial shipping pass through the Strait of Hormuz.

For weeks, Trump publicly signaled he was considering a return to large-scale combat operations after the midterm elections, and the head of CENTCOM, Adm. Brad Cooper, met with Trump, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, and Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Dan Caine last week.

If the Trump administration opts to return to major combat operations, airstrikes against air defense targets, such as those referenced by Trump, could help facilitate the operation.

“I’m not looking to, you know, kill lots of people, but if we have to, we’ll have to,” Trump told Fox News. “But I’m not looking to do that. And we’re very strong right now.”

Iran signaled it would respond to any further U.S. military actions.

“We are still in a state of war, and from the Islamic Republic of Iran’s perspective, the aggression against our country has not ended,” Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said Nov. 3, according to Iranian state media. “As long as the military aggression has not come to a complete and permanent end, the Islamic Republic of Iran retains its right to legitimate self-defense.”

The post US Conducts Airstrikes on Iran, Latest in Series of Undisclosed Attacks appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine.

item.title: Ex-CSO Saltzman to Lead Advisory Board at Voyager Technologies
item.dc:creator: Greg Hadley
item.description:
In his first professional move since retiring from the Space Force at the end of August, former Chief of Space Operations Gen. B. Chance Saltzman will lead the board of advisors for Voyager Technologies, the firm announced Nov. 2.

The post Ex-CSO Saltzman to Lead Advisory Board at Voyager Technologies appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine.
item.content:encoded:
In his first professional move since retiring from the Space Force at the end of August, former Chief of Space Operations Gen. B. Chance Saltzman will lead the board of advisors for Voyager Technologies, the firm announced Nov. 2.

Launched as a holding company in 2019 to acquire and run space-focused subsidiaries, Voyager has started to position itself to compete for programs that are Space Force priorities, including space-based missile interceptors, satellite communications, AI, and more.

Voyager’s biggest contracts to date have been with NASA. The firm is developing a commercial space station to go in low-Earth orbit called Starlab through its subsidiary Nanoracks and is providing lunar landers for the Commercial Lunar Payload Services program through its subsidiary Astrobotic Technology.

Now its defense business is starting to grow too. Last December, it won a $21 million contract from the Air Force Research Laboratory to develop AI-enabled intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance systems. In May, Anduril Industries named Voyager a partner in its effort to develop space-based interceptors. In August, the company announced a contract with the Space Force to develop a datalink between satellites. And in October, the Pentagon’s Strategic Capabilities Office awarded Voyager a $22.4 million contract for “next-generation satellite deployment systems.”

Matt Magana, president of the company’s defense and national security business, told Air & Space Forces Magazine last year that it views the technologies that will be key to creating the Golden Dome missile defense system, such as propulsion and artificial intelligence, as similiarly high-interest for non-defense customers.

With Saltzman on its advisory panel, Voyager gains “strategic counsel for the company’s space and defense efforts,” the company said in a release. In nearly four years as CSO, Saltzman emphasized that space is now a warfighting domain, and that the Space Force needed to rapidly grow to be able to operate effectively even while under attack.

In a statement, Saltzman indicated he sees Voyager’s defense business continuing to grow.

“The national security space mission is expanding faster than industry can currently meet it,” Saltzman said. “Voyager has the technology, the agility, and the ambition to help close that gap, and I’m looking forward to helping the team turn that potential into capability for our services.”

It’s common for Pentagon leaders to join commercial firms in advisory and senior roles after retiring. Saltzman’s predecessor, Gen. John W. “Jay” Raymond is on the board of satellite imagery company Planet Labs, for example, as well as space mobility firm Impulse Space, among others. Saltzman, like any former service chief, is limited from lobbying in the Pentagon on behalf of commercial entities for two years after leaving office, but is free to act in an advisory role on matters of strategic direction, technology develoopment or investment decisions.

The post Ex-CSO Saltzman to Lead Advisory Board at Voyager Technologies appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine.

item.title: Air Force Now Offers Free Wi-Fi in Dorms on 25 Bases with More to Come
item.dc:creator: Matthew Cox
item.description:
Airmen can now tap into free high-speed Wi-Fi in dormitories at 25 Air Force bases with more installations scheduled to come online, through a deal with with internet provider Boingo Wireless.

The post Air Force Now Offers Free Wi-Fi in Dorms on 25 Bases with More to Come appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine.
item.content:encoded:
Airmen can now tap into free high-speed Wi-Fi in dormitories at 25 Air Force bases with more installations scheduled to come online, through a deal with with internet provider Boingo Wireless.

The contract, run by the Army & Air Force Exchanged Service, taps into Boingo’s existing Wi-Fi infrastructure at bases across the U.S., plus one in Japan, according to an Oct. 29 announcement from Boingo.

Task & Purpose first reported on the announcement.

Currently, free Wi-Fi is available in dorms at 25 installations, according to an AAFES spokesperson:

  • Altus Air Force Base, Okla.
  • Beale Air Force Base, Calif.
  • Camp Bullis at Joint Base San Antonio, Texas
  • Cannon Air Force Base, N.M.
  • Columbus Air Force Base, Miss.
  • Davis-Monthan Air Force Base, Ariz.
  • Dyess Air Force Base, Texas
  • Eglin Air Force Base, Fla.
  • Ellsworth Air Force Base, S.D.
  • Fairchild Air Force Base, Wash.
  • Goodfellow Air Force Base, Texas
  • Joint Base San Antonio-Lackland, Texas
  • Kirtland Air Force Base, N.M.
  • Little Rock Air Force Base, Ark.
  • Luke Air Force Base, Ariz.
  • Maxwell Air Force Base and Gunter Annex, Ala.
  • McChord Field at Joint Base Lewis-McChord, Wash.
  • McConnell Air Force Base, Kan.
  • Misawa Air Base, Japan
  • Offutt Air Force Base, Neb.
  • Scott Air Force Base, Ill.
  • Sheppard Air Force Base, Texas
  • United States Air Force Academy, Colo.
  • Vance Air Force Base, Okla.
  • Vandenberg Space Force Base, Calif.

The AAFES spokesperson added that Wi-Fi will also soon be available at Holloman Air Force Base, N.M. Holloman still requires network configuration and service “is expected to be available within 30 to 45 days after the memorandum of agreement is executed,” the spokesperson said.

It’s unclear what other installations will get free Wi-Fi in the future under the Boingo contract, but the telecommunications firm’s announcement states that the deal includes “additional site deployments systematically underway to expand coverage.”

“Staying connected to family and friends makes a difference in Airmen’s daily lives and helps them stay mission ready,” Air Force Chief Master Sgt. Angela Holden, AAFES’ senior enlisted advisor, said in Boingo’s announcement. “This initiative is one more way the Exchange supports quality of life for Airmen while helping them feel more at home in their dorms.”

The AAFES contract with Boingo fulfills congressional guidance for the services to provide free Wi-Fi for service members that appeared in the 2025 National Defense Authorization Act.

“The Secretary of a military department may provide, to a member of the armed forces who resides in military unaccompanied housing (as defined in section 2871 of this title) within the United States, broadband internet access service, at no cost to such member,” according to the legislation.

The Air Force has acknowledged in the past that access to the internet is an essential tool for continued learning. “It would not be a blanket statement to say the whole Air Force [now] understands that … Wi-Fi is a necessity, as opposed to a convenience,” Lt. Gen. Marshall B. Webb, then-commander of Air Education and Training Command at Joint Base San Antonio-Randolph, Texas said in 2021.

The post Air Force Now Offers Free Wi-Fi in Dorms on 25 Bases with More to Come appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine.

item.title: General Atomics, AFRL Eye Next Steps for Autonomous Drone Concepts
item.dc:creator: Steve Losey
item.description:
General Atomics, the maker of one of the Air Force’s first Collaborative Combat Aircraft, has ambitious plans for its family of semi-autonomous drones beyond the FQ-42, including a flying-wing aircraft capable of carrying out both reconnaissance and strike missions. Meanwhile, the Air Force Research Laboratory announced a new program to test mission systems for autonomous aircraft, particularly those meant for reconnaissance. The lab recently flew General Atomics’ CCA prototype, the XQ-67A, as part of the program.

The post General Atomics, AFRL Eye Next Steps for Autonomous Drone Concepts appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine.
item.content:encoded:
General Atomics, the maker of one of the Air Force’s first Collaborative Combat Aircraft, has ambitious plans for its family of semi-autonomous drones beyond the FQ-42, including a flying-wing aircraft capable of carrying out both reconnaissance and strike missions.

Meanwhile, the Air Force Research Laboratory announced a new program to test mission systems for autonomous aircraft, particularly those meant for reconnaissance. The lab recently flew General Atomics’ CCA prototype, the XQ-67A, as part of the program.

General Atomics spokesman C. Mark Brinkley told Air & Space Forces Magazine in an email the company is working on an uncrewed flying wing design it calls NextGen. The War Zone first reported on the NextGen aircraft.

Brinkley stressed that NextGen is “not a CCA,” but instead a “much larger … fully armed, fully outfitted, [intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance]/strike wing” aircraft. NextGen will use a hybrid-electric propulsion system that could allow it to fly more than 60 hours without being refueled, he said, and have the potential to be flown remotely, autonomously, or semi-autonomously.

Brinkley said NextGen is planned as a “high-end capability,” and work on that program will feed into another, smaller flying wing drone that would be part of General Atomics’ Gambit series of drones.

The Gambit concept, unveiled in 2022, is envisioned as a family of modular airframes that can all fit a common “chassis” that includes a common engine, landing gear, and processors. The FQ-42 CCA is part of that series.

General Atomics refers to its future flying wing concept, which NextGen could inform, as Gambit 4.

Gambit 4 would cost less than NextGen, Brinkley said, but would also have shorter endurance and less-effective stealth capabilities.

“I don’t think people realize how deep GA-ASI’s bandwidth is, or how much we dedicate to R&D,” Brinkley said. “NextGen is coming, and the work we’re doing on that flying wing program will funnel into Gambit 4 so that when customers are ready for this, we’re not starting from scratch here either.”

General Atomics received a $99.3 million contract from AFRL in May 2025 to build a long-endurance, autonomous flying wing aircraft that could fly reconaissance and strike missions, called GHOST. That award announcement described GHOST using language similar to how General Atomics now refers to NextGen, including a references to its hybrid-electric propulsion system. Brinkley declined to comment on any potential relationship between GHOST and NextGen.

Another planned Gambit drone, called Gambit 6, would be a ground strike variant of the FQ-42. Brinkley said General Atomics is planning to hold a live-fire event with one of its own Gambit 6 aircraft in early 2027, using a ground attack munition.

“Every Gambit variant feeds expertise into the other variants by default,” Brinkley said. “So the work ongoing now for live-fire on FQ-42 Vengeance, coupled with years of internal air-to-ground launches from MQ-20 Avenger, allows us to rapidly reconfigure for Gambit 6.”

Brinkley said the FQ-42’s ability to carry weapons in its internal weapons bay will make it stealthier and more survivable than if it had to carry weapons on its wing. Other nations that are considering the CCA concept will need them to carry out air-to-ground missions, Brinkley said, making them possible customers for Gambit 6.

General Atomics is also working on another Gambit concept, similar to the FQ-42 or Gambit 6, that would be optimized for navies around the world to use on ships. This idea, called Gambit 5, would need to include the proper landing gear, equipment compatible with catapults and arresting gear, and would have to be resistant to the corrosive salt-heavy environment that comes with operating at sea, Brinkley said.

General Atomics is also developing a concept for a red air trainer drone, which could act as an adversary while training new pilots, as part of its Gambit series. Brinkley said that will be critical to teach future pilots how to fight against enemies that fly their own CCA-type drones.

“Eventually, manned aircraft will need to fight against these autonomous jets and train like they fight, but you don’t need them actually loaded with weapons,” Brinkley said. “You’ll be simulating all of that anyway. So with Gambit 3, you can alter the design without starting from scratch and probably remove some fighter components from the trainers to add overall value.”

The XQ-67, General Atomics’ first Gambit drone, is showing ways such semi-autonomous aircraft could be used in a future war. AFRL said in an Oct. 27 statement that it and the Air Force’s Experimental Operations Unit had recently flown the XQ-67 in the Nevada Test and Training Range.

AFRL was not able to immediately answer further questions about the flight, but did say it demonstrated how the XQ-67 can integrate advanced mission systems that would “work collaboratively in demanding combat environments.” Those systems include advanced sensors, mission computers, and power and thermal management hardware.

AFRL said that integrating beyond line-of-sight datalinks and “live, virtual and constructive simulations” during the flight showed how uncrewed platforms could be operated across distributed theaters.

“This proved that AFRL’s autonomous architectures, aligned with autonomy and agile mission suite government reference architectures, can reliably process and relay combat-relevant data in real-world scenarios,” Trenton White, an aerospace engineer in AFRL’s air warfare directorate, said in the release.

The flight was carried out under a project called “Demon APE,” which is short for Demonstration of ACP Performance and Effectiveness.

In a video on Demon APE, the lab said the program particularly focuses on improving battlespace awareness by linking together autonomous drones that specialize in reconnaissance, with the goal of integrating them with manned aircraft such as fighters and bombers and making them more lethal.

“By pairing AFRL’s rapid prototyping with ACC’s operational test units, the Air Force is shortening the timeline between concept and warfighter capability,” Col. Matthew Caspers, Department of the Air Force deputy technology executive officer for air, said in AFRL’s statement.

Brinkley praised AFRL’s work partnering with General Atomics on the XQ-67, and said the lab “really [has] a vision for this as a new warfighting concept for the future.”

The post General Atomics, AFRL Eye Next Steps for Autonomous Drone Concepts appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine.

item.title: T-38 Crash That Briefly Paused Flights Caused by ‘Under-Torqued’ Pin
item.dc:creator: Greg Hadley
item.description:
The crash of a T-38 trainer jet this May—which caused a weekslong pause in flights across the fleet—was caused by an improperly installed pin for one of the jet’s horizontal stabilizers, according to a new accident report released Oct. 30. When the pin disengaged midflight, it created the slightest amount of “play” in the system, which in turn caused aerodynamic flutter that shook the aircraft until both stabilizers were ripped off.

The post T-38 Crash That Briefly Paused Flights Caused by ‘Under-Torqued’ Pin appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine.
item.content:encoded:
The crash of a T-38 trainer jet this May—which caused a weekslong pause in flights across the fleet—was caused by an improperly installed pin for one of the jet’s horizontal stabilizers, according to a new accident report released Oct. 30. When the pin disengaged midflight, it created the slightest amount of “play” in the system, which in turn caused aerodynamic flutter that shook the aircraft until both stabilizers were ripped off.

The aircraft was destroyed in the mishap, with the loss valued at $11.3 million. The USAF instructor and international student pilot successfully ejected and suffered minor injuries.

Investigators determined the contractors responsible for maintenance on the T-38 out of Columbus Air Force Base, Miss., failed to perform a check for play, or “backlash,” after installing a new actuator during unscheduled work in the weeks before the crash, and their supervisors missed the mistake.

“The contractors signing off the actuator installation, the work center supervisor, the Impoundment Official, Quality Assurance personnel, and the Impoundment Release Authority had the opportunity and capability to identify this missing required check, but did not,” the president of the Accident Investigation Board concluded.

The investigation also cleared the crew of contributing to the mishap in any way.

A Tenth of an Inch

The T-38’s horizontal stabilizers control the pitch of the aircraft’s nose, driven by two actuators on either side. The actuators work against each other to twist steel torque tubes so that the stabilizers remain in tension and don’t flutter.

All it takes to disrupt this system is a little bit of wiggle—no more than 0.1 inches of play or backlash in the actuator, according to a technical report reviewed by investigators. Once that happens, the torque tubes can lose tension and the stabilizers can start to flutter, “an aerodynamic feedback loop where fast-moving air increasingly shakes an aircraft structure until it breaks,” the report explained.

That’s what happened just before noon on May 12, after a fourship of T-38s took off from Columbus as part of a fighter-bomber fundamentals training sortie. The group was just starting with a G-warmup turn when the instructor and student in one plane heard a loud noise and the aircraft began to shudder. They then “reported strong vibrations and negative G, with the [student pilot] being lifted out of his seat,” the report states.

The instructor pilot took control of the aircraft and tried to level off, but the noises and shudders continued, followed by an “uncommanded pitch downwards with a spike in negative G.” Even with the control stick pulled fully back, the report noted, the aircraft continued to plunge downward—the horizontal stabilizers had been ripped off.

The ejection wasn’t completely smooth. While the instructor pilot got out cleanly, one of the student pilot’s leg restraints was later found to be twisted, and he reported pain in his left calf.

The aircraft, meanwhile, hit the ground in rural Alabama and became a fiery wreck.

Maintenance

A month prior to the mishap, the T-38 in question had been impounded “for an uncommanded 130-degree roll to the right,” according to the report. In attempting to troubleshoot the issue, maintenance personnel removed and reinstalled the aft fuselage, sometimes called the boattail, and discovered that the right horizontal stabilizer’s travel, or range of motion, was “out of limits.”

Maintainers performed a backlash check on the right stabilizer, but then subsequently determined the left stabilizer’s actuator also had “excessive play.” The actuator was removed, repaired, and reinstalled—but crucially, personnel never performed another backlash test.

Instead, maintainers ran checks to ensure the “travel” or range of motion on both right and left stabilizers was within limits and, with a few other checks and repairs, released the T-38 from impound. On May 1, the jet cleared a restricted check flight.

The accident investigation board did not conclude why the crucial backlash check never happened but faulted the entire maintenance team for “compliance failures.”

The Air Force Research Laboratory ran an analysis of all the recovered bolts, nuts, and pins from the mishap, and determined they had all failed because of the “overload” of the flutter. But investigators did not recover the aft actuator pin for the left horizontal stabilizer, and they noted that its “nut and stud remained riveted … with intact threads,” suggesting the pin had been under-torqued and came loose.

Investigators did not give any possible explanation for why the pin had been under-torqued.

Weekslong Pause

A week after the May 12 crash, on May 19, the Air Force announced a fleetwide operational pause affecting units within Air Education and Training Command, Air Combat Command, Air Force Materiel Command, and Air Force Global Strike Command.

On May 28, the service lifted the operational pause as it began inspecting T-38s, with the goal of returning to flight within days.Officials offered no further updates after that.

The T-38—a supersonic trainer first fielded in the 1960s and used by the Air Force to teach future fighter and bomber pilots—remains one of the oldest aircraft in the USAF fleet, and officials cite problems maintaining it as a key reason the service needs to transition to the T-7A Red Hawk, a modernized advanced trainer.

The post T-38 Crash That Briefly Paused Flights Caused by ‘Under-Torqued’ Pin appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine.

item.title: NORAD F-16s Test Homeland Defense Mission at Remote Alaskan Island
item.dc:creator: Steve Losey
item.description:
The Air Force in October carried out a homeland defense mission, with jets including F-16 Fighting Falcons, in Alaska’s remote Aleutian Islands to show a base there could safeguard the northern regions.

The post NORAD F-16s Test Homeland Defense Mission at Remote Alaskan Island appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine.
item.content:encoded:
The Air Force in October carried out a homeland defense mission, with jets including F-16 Fighting Falcons, in Alaska’s remote Aleutian Islands to show a base there could safeguard the northern regions.

The North American Aerospace Defense Command, or NORAD, said in an Oct. 30 statement that the F-16s first maintained an air defense alert during a deployment to Eareckson Air Station, Alaska, from Oct. 18 to 26, in a mission called Operation Noble Defender. 

Noble Defender transitioned to a new homeland defense operation, called Noble Eagle, which took place Oct. 25. Noble Eagle was a coordinated U.S.-Canadian operation, including two F-16s, F-35 Lightning IIs from Eielson Air Force Base, Alaska, and Royal Canadian Air Force CF-18 Hornets from Cold Lake, Alberta.

It also included an E-3 Sentry—also known as an AWACS, for Airborne Warning and Control System—from Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson, Alaska, several KC-135 Stratotankers and a CC-150 Polaris to conduct aerial refueling, and an HC-130 Combat King II in case search-and-rescue and personnel recovery missions needed to be launched.

“Defending North America demands speed, flexibility, and the ability to bring combat power together across vast distances,” Air Force Lt. Gen. Robert Davis, the commander of NORAD’s Alaskan region, said in the statement. “Operating from Eareckson Air Station proved we can deploy to an austere location, maintain alert, launch on short notice, and seamlessly integrate U.S. and Canadian forces to defend the northern approaches.”

Air National Guardsmen from Elmendorf’s 176th Wing, including communications and cyber systems experts, set up outdoor equipment to maintain rapid, resilient communications during Noble Defender, photographs released by the Air Force showed.

Noble Defender is a recurring air defense operation that NORAD said demonstrates its ability to defend the U.S. and Canada from threats, while strengthening the two nations’ partnerships and binational NORAD commands.

During the F-16s’ deployment to Eareckson, the air station’s arresting system was successfully certified, NORAD said. This underscored Eareckson could be a viable location to launch future fighter operations, despite it being an austere, remote airfield, the command said. 

Eareckson is located on Shemya Island, a tiny land mass of less than six square miles near the western tip of the Aleutians. Its primary mission is to serve as a remote missile defense and surveillance outpost. It is also the home of an important radar system called COBRA DANE, which can track ballistic missile launches from up to 2,000 miles away.

Eareckson is about 1,600 miles from Eielson, and 2,600 miles from Cold Lake, which NORAD said highlighted “the scale across which NORAD synchronized the force.”

It is also less than 300 miles away from Russia’s eastern coast, and a little more than 2,000 miles away from North Korea, making its location vital for the U.S. early warning mission.

item.title: Space Force Weighs Proliferated Cislunar Satellite Constellation
item.dc:creator: Courtney Albon
item.description:
The Space Force is considering launching up to five satellites to cislunar space as soon as 2029 to help lay the foundation for a future proliferated constellation between Earth and the moon. 

The post Space Force Weighs Proliferated Cislunar Satellite Constellation appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine.
item.content:encoded:
The Space Force is considering launching up to five satellites to cislunar space as soon as 2029 to help lay the foundation for a future proliferated constellation between Earth and the moon. 

In a Nov. 2 industry notice, the service said it is “notionally interested” in launching a handful of satellites to inform a future acquisition strategy for a Cislunar Space System to operate beyond geosynchronous orbit. The spacecraft should be ready to launch by late 2029 for initial operations by 2031. 

“These vehicles may serve as seed vehicles that will inform the acquisition strategy for a potential future proliferated cislunar constellation,” the notice states. “The government is looking for information on industry’s ability to provide a rapid, low-risk solution.”

The notice comes amid what Space Force leaders have described as a significant shift in the U.S. military’s posture toward cislunar. In an Oct. 21 speech at AFCEA’s Space Industry Days conference, Maj. Gen. Stephen Purdy, who oversees the Space Force’s advanced programs acquisition portfolio, said that as recently as January, he was told to avoid talking about plans for cislunar systems and strategy. Now, leadership across the Department of Defense are leaning in, discussing the region as a “warfighting domain” and pushing for projects to enable operations there. 

That momentum is in part driven by China’s move toward the moon, a vision that not only includes lunar landers and a military presence, but work to establish models for positioning, navigation, and timing within the next 10 years, and launch an international lunar research station. 

“They’re not planning for a one-off demo,” Purdy said. “They are planning for sustained activity. It’s in their strategic documents … and they’re building the R&D and the S&T and the operational reps and set to get all those missions done.”

Cislunar space is hundreds of thousands of kilometers in distance and its volume is 1,728 times that of geosynchronous orbit. Space systems operating in the region must contend with the combined gravitational characteristics of both the Earth and the Moon as well as unpredictable orbits that require constant station-keeping. Cislunar also lacks its own positioning, navigation, and timing grid—offices like the National Geospatial Intelligence Agency are working to establish that framework.

The Space Force’s notice to industry doesn’t spell out what types of payloads the satellites might carry, though officials have said they’re particularly interested in space domain awareness, PNT, and communications in the cislunar regime. The notice says the Space Force is interested in satellites equipped with propulsion systems that can support its station-keeping requirements as well as orbital transfers. The service also wants information on AI and compute capabilities that can support long-duration autonomous operations.

Purdy said the Space Force plans to act quickly and wants to take advantage of commercially available technology. According to the notice, the service could award up to five contracts and may aim to start funding initial design work as soon as early next year.

“We’re looking for existing commercial or near-commercial means, non-developmental solutions, hardware with actual relevant evidence behind it, software that doesn’t need a huge amount of work … and ground systems,” Purdy said. “This isn’t a four- or five-year science project. This is about getting capability out soon.”

The post Space Force Weighs Proliferated Cislunar Satellite Constellation appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine.

item.title: Key Midterm Election Races to Watch for the Air Force and Space Force
item.dc:creator: Greg Hadley
item.description:
Dozens of former Airmen are running for Congress in the 2026 midterms, with Election Day fast approaching on Nov. 3. But the potential impact of the election for the Air Force and Space Force goes beyond just the number of former service members on Capitol Hill—the results will also decide the people who advocate for local installations, conduct oversight, and set policy through legislation.

The post Key Midterm Election Races to Watch for the Air Force and Space Force appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine.
item.content:encoded:
Dozens of former Airmen are running for Congress in the 2026 midterms, but as Election Day arrives Nov. 3, the election’s impact on the Air Force and Space Force figures to resonate beyond just the number of former service members on Capitol Hill.

In the House of Representatives, Rep. Rob Wittman (R-Va.) is locked in a tight race with Democratic challenger Shannon Taylor. Polls show the two candidates separated by just a few points, and election handicappers rate the race as a toss-up.

Wittman is vice chair of the House Armed Services Committee and has an outsized influence on Air Force policy as chair of the tactical air and land forces subcommittee. Earlier this year, as part of the committee’s work on the 2027 defense policy bill, he pushed to authorize the Pentagon to make multiyear procurement deals for both the F-35 and F-15EX fighters and he has supported continued procurement of the E-7 Wedgetail early warning and battle management aircraft.

If Wittman prevails, he would be a key to succeed Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Ala.) as HASC chair, if the Republicans maintain their majority, or to become the ranking member if the Democrats gain the majority. Rogers is term-limited from retaining the chair by Republican conference rules, but he has said he would seek a waiver to hold onto his leadership position. Other contenders include Rep. Ronny Jackson (R-Texas) and Rep. Trent Kelly (R-Miss.).

But if Wittman loses and the Democrats win control of the House, current ranking Democrat Rep. Adam Smith (D-Wash.) would likely return to the chair, a position he held when the Democrats last held the majority.

Other competitive races that could affect HASC members:

  • Rep. Michael Turner (R-Ohio), who chaired the tactical air and land forces subcommittee prior to Wittman and represents Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, is running against an Air Force vet, former Maj. Kristina Knickerbocker. Turner is slightly favored, but a recent poll indicated the race appeared to be tightening.
  • Rep. Jeff Crank (R-Colo.), whose district includes the U.S. Air Force Academy, Peterson Space Force Base, and Schriever Space Force Base, is running against Jessica Killin, a U.S. Army veteran. Polls show an extremely close race, which experts recently rated a “toss-up.”
  • Rep. Don Davis (D-N.C.), just the the fourth U.S. Air Force Academy graduate ever elected to Congress and a former captain, is facing retired Army Col. Laurie Buckhout in the most expensive House race in the country. Polls are all over the map on this one. The winner will represent Seymour-Johnson Air Force Base, the heart of the Air Force’s F-15 training enterprise.

While the HASC handles policy and oversight, the House Appropriations Committee and its defense subcommittee is responsible for the funding that goes to the Air Force, Space Force, and the Pentagon. And the chair of that defense subcommittee is locked in an unusual election battle. As a result of redistricting in California, Rep. Ken Calvert is running against another Republican, Rep. Young Kim. While the seat is guaranteed to stay red, a Calvert loss would shake up the defense appropriations subcommittee.

Other members of the House Appropriations defense subcommittee in competitive races include Reps. David Valadao (D-Calif.), Marcy Kaptur (D-Ohio), and Henry Cuellar (D-Texas).

In the Senate

Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine), chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, is locked in an extremely close race with challenger Troy Jackson. Collins is also a member of the Senate Appropriations defense subcommittee, which wields enormous influence over Pentagon funding.

Also on the defense subcommittee is Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith (R-Miss.), who is in a closer-than-expected race with challenger Scott Colom. Hyde-Smith is favored, but the race is closely watched.

Meanwhile, Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.), current chair of the Senate Appropriations defense subcommittee, is retiring. It is unclear who might replace him on that panel if Republicans hold the Senate, but if Democrats flip the chamber, Sen. Christopher Coons (D-Del.) will likely become chair.

The Senate Armed Services Committee also faces turnover, with more than a fifth of the panel’s 27 members either not running for reelection or facing a significant challenge. Four members of the SASC are not running: Sens. Gary Peters (D-Mich.), Joni Ernst (R-Iowa), Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.), and Tommy Tuberville (R-Ala.). Two more are in competitive races: Sens. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska) and Ashley Moody (R-Fla.)

Thinking Local

Districts that represent represent communities surrounding military installations are also in play. Such legislators often become involved in funnelling resources to bases, whether to fund new construction, units, or equipment, including aircraft.

For the Air Force and Space Force, Senate battlegrounds Alaska, Kansas, Texas, Ohio, Michigan, and Florida all include major bases. Alaska in particular has key Space Force radars and Air Force fifth-generation fighters, Texas has the services’ Basic Military Training and Air Education and Training Command, and Florida includes the rapidly expanding eastern range for space launch and major Air Force bases for testing, F-35s, tankers, and special operations.

On a more granular level, other bases in competitive House districts include:

  • MacDill Air Force Base, Fla.: Incumbent Rep. Kathy Castor (D) is in a tight content with Mike Beltran (R).
  • Joint Base Lindsey Graham, S.C.: The seat is open with the departure of Rep. Nancy Mace, and retired Navy Vice Adm. Nancy Lacore (D) is going up against Jenny Costa Honeycutt (R).
  • Davis-Monthan Air Force Base, Ariz.: Incumbent Rep. Juan Ciscomani (R) is considered a slight underdog to JoAnna Mendoza.
  • Joint Base San Antonio-Raldolph, Texas: as part of redistricting, JBSA-Randolph is now in a district with an open seat. Air Force vet Carlos De La Cruz is the Republican nominee.

The post Key Midterm Election Races to Watch for the Air Force and Space Force appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine.
